vignette:
Erin is a 37-year-old musician who came to treatment months after a bombing at an outdoor summer concert where she had been performing. She still describes the evening in unnervingly precise detail: the heat coming off the stage lights, the metallic smell in the air after the blast, and most of all the bitter chemical taste that flooded her mouth when she fell and realized people were screaming and running. In the chaos that followed, that taste seemed to brand the moment into her. She remembers seeing the crowd buckle and scatter, hearing equipment crash, and for seconds at a time feeling as if the world had turned unreal while her senses became painfully sharp. Since then, when the memory returns, it does not feel like a thought about something that happened. It feels present again, fully real, as if she is back inside the scene with the same taste in her mouth and the same sensory force all at once.

In the weeks after the attack, Erin tried to return to rehearsing and performing, telling herself that music was the only stable part of her life. Instead, she found that she could not hold her attention where she wanted it. The more on guard she felt in rehearsal rooms and clubs, the less the bombing stayed contained as a past event; being keyed up seemed to pull the scene closer, until the memory would break through with little warning. During practice she would lose track of the bar she was playing, miss cues, and snap at bandmates for small mistakes. She became increasingly keyed up in crowded venues, scanning faces and noises rather than listening to what was in front of her. In those moments of strain, the concert no longer stayed in the past. A burst of feedback, the jolt of a subwoofer, or the stale taste of beer at a club could pull her abruptly into a flashback so complete that she would grip her instrument as if bracing for another explosion. Her difficulty concentrating and her irritability seemed to keep her near the edge of the event, and from that edge the memory came back with even more force.

What has taken hold most deeply, though, is what Erin believes the bombing revealed. She had once felt at home in music scenes, festivals, and crowds; now she says she belongs nowhere. The places that used to organize her life feel contaminated, and she has come to view strangers with suspicion, certain that people are not what they seem and that danger can sit unnoticed inside an ordinary audience. When she talks about the future, her voice flattens. She cannot picture one. Those convictions seem to give the memory a new kind of permanence: she goes over the event not to understand it but as if it proves, again and again, that the world has already ended in the essential way. The more hopeless and cut off she feels, the more fixed and vivid the bombing becomes in her mind, preserved in exact detail rather than softening into the past.

That same vividness then feeds those beliefs back to her. When a flashback hits and she can taste the air from that night and feel the scene across all her senses, Erin is left convinced that the attack is not really over and that she herself has been permanently altered by it. Afterward she is shaken and ashamed by how completely she disappeared into it. She reads the force of the reliving as evidence that she is no longer like other people, that she cannot safely belong in the ordinary world of rehearsals, green rooms, and crowded bars where musicians work. Each episode seems to harden her distrust as well; if the memory can overtake her in the middle of a set or while loading gear past unfamiliar men lingering near a venue entrance, then to her that means vigilance is justified and the future is already narrowed to endurance rather than possibility.

Her relationship has begun to strain under this pattern. Her partner has tried to encourage her to take smaller gigs again, but Erin often comes home angry, unable to explain why a sound check or the smell of spilled alcohol set her off. She is quick-tempered in ways that frighten her, and afterward she withdraws, convinced no one around her can really understand what it is like to be transported back without warning. She misses notes in rehearsal because her mind splinters; then she sees the frustration on other musicians’ faces and takes it as further proof that there is no place left where she fits.

By the time she sought help, Erin was still performing only sporadically and dreading every commitment she accepted. What finally brought her in was a recent club date where a burst of amplifier noise sent her into such a vivid reliving that she stopped mid-song, tasting the blast in her mouth, certain for a second that the audience was about to stampede. She left the stage furious and humiliated. Sitting in the intake, she said she was afraid she had no future at all—not just as a musician, but as a person who could ever feel part of the world again. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not confidence or even comfort at first, but the chance to remember that night without feeling swallowed by it.

violations.explanation: The vignette describes threat arising during flashbacks and from beliefs about danger, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Erin’s sense of threat drives or leads to the trauma memory returning.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: The vignette describes threat arising during flashbacks and from beliefs about danger, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Erin’s sense of threat drives or leads to the trauma memory returning.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
